paper_title: DepthGraft: Structural Regularization through Hierarchical Cross-Layer KV Reconstruction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Scaling depth is a key route to stronger large language models, but Pre-LN architectures often suffer from depth-wise information dilution, limiting the effective use of deep layers. While cross-layer connectivity has proven effective at mitigating this problem, existing designs usually introduce additional computation or memory access. We revisit cross-layer KV sharing as an efficient form of such connectivity. Beyond cache compression, each KV reuse edge creates a direct gradient path from deep layers to source KV projections, turning KV sharing into an implicit structural regularizer for KV representation geometry. We provide a systematic analysis of this mechanism, showing that proper sharing topologies sharpen key retrieval directions while enriching the value content subspace, whereas existing adjacent or global-anchor designs do not fully exploit this effect. Motivated by this, we propose DepthGraft, a hierarchical KV-sharing architecture that reconstructs deep-layer KV from stride-aligned shallow-middle source pairs. DepthGraft distributes non-local gradient flow across source layers, while preserving prefill early completion and reducing KV cache by roughly one third. Experiments on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters show consistent downstream improvements under both GQA and MLA. Notably, on the 16B MoE model, DepthGraft achieves a 7.0% absolute improvement on MMLU-Pro, along with gains of 6.6% on CMMLU and 6.4% on C3. These results validate the potential of DepthGraft as a scalable design for large-scale pretraining. The project page is available at https://github.com/jianke0604/DepthGraft.

Introduction Scaling depth has been primary lever for improving Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) [21, 32, 42]. In modern Pre-Layer-Normalization Transformers [40], however, adding layers does not always yield the expected improvements [11, 22]. The residual stream [12] aggregates all preceding computations through single hidden-state trajectory with fixed additive updates; as the stack grows deeper, features formed in early layers can be progressively diluted and become difficult for later layers to retrieve. This depth-wise information dilution limits the effective use of additional layers, making depth scaling less efficient than its representational capacity would suggest [9, 30]. Recent work has validated cross-layer connectivity as an effective remedy for information dilution along depth. Instead of forcing all depth history through the residual stream, recent designs allow deep layers to directly read earlier representations: Attention Residuals [33] reweights preceding hidden states to replace fixed residual accumulation, while Mixture-of-Depths Attention (MoDA) [48] augments attention with keyvalue pairs from previous layers. Such connections give deep layers direct access to earlier features and create shorter gradient paths to shallow layers. However, dense cross-layer access also introduces additional computation, memory traffic, and system complexity, requiring careful performanceefficiency trade-offs and sophisticated systems-level engineering. We note that cross-layer KV sharing can also be viewed as form of such connectivity: it provides deep layers with channel that bypasses information dilution in the residual stream by granting direct access to shallow-layer memory representations, while gradients flow from deep layers back through the shared KV to shallow layers, supplying shallow-layer KV with optimization signals driven by deep-layer task demandsthus holding the potential to improve depth utilization. Although cross-layer KV sharing has been explored in prior work [4, 31, 49], existing methods predominantly approach it from the perspective of cache compression and inference acceleration. No prior work has systematically studied the cross-layer gradient dynamics of KV sharing, especially how such connections reshape KV representation geometry during pretraining and how the sharing topology determines this effect. In this paper, we propose that KV sharing is not merely cache-saving mechanism, but also form of cross-layer gradient regularization. When source layers KV is reused by distant deep layer, the source KV receives training signals from multiple query spaces. This reshapes KV representation geometry in an asymmetric way: keys are encouraged to concentrate around shared discriminative retrieval directions, while values are pushed to cover richer content subspace. With proper sharing topology, this specialization sharpens memory retrieval while increasing the expressive capacity of the value content channel, yielding useful structural bias for training. We use this lens to revisit existing KV-sharing methods and find that their topologies expose complementary limitations. Adjacent-layer sharing provides too little query-space separation, whereas global-anchor sharing concentrates heterogeneous deep-layer gradients on few sources, preventing either design from fully exploiting the regularization effect. Motivated by this analysis, we propose DepthGraft, simple hierarchical KV-sharing design derived from the cross-layer regularization view. DepthGraft partitions the network into shallow, middle, and deep stages. The shallow and middle stages compute KV normally, while each deep layer reconstructs its KV from stride-aligned shallowmiddle source pair using learnable channel-wise coefficients. This construction creates non-local sourcereuse connections with sufficient query-space separation, distributes cross-layer gradients across many source layers rather than few global anchors, and gives each deep layer access to 2 memory bases at two abstraction levels. As result, DepthGraft preserves the efficiency benefits of KV sharing, including prefill early completion and KV-cache reduction, while turning the memory pathway into an effective regularized cross-layer connection. Training-dynamics analyses further support our theory, showing that DepthGraft reshapes KV representation geometry as predicted, and experiments across dense and MoE models demonstrate consistent performance gains at multiple scales. Our main contributions are as follows. 1). KV sharing as cross-layer gradient regularization. We identify KV sharing as form of cross-layer connectivity and provide systematic analysis of how its gradient paths reshape KV geometry. Our analysis shows that proper KV sharing sharpens key retrieval directions while enriching the value content subspace, and that this effect is governed by the sharing topology. 2). Hierarchical cross-layer KV reconstruction. We propose DepthGraft, which uses hierarchical stage layout to reconstruct deep-layer KV from stride-aligned shallowmiddle source pairs. This yields distributed non-local connectivity pattern with two abstraction-level memory bases, avoiding the concentrated-anchor structure of prior KV-sharing methods. 3). Efficient and scalable implementation. DepthGraft removes independent KV materialization from the deep stage, reducing KV cache by roughly 1 3 and allowing KV construction to finish before the final stage during prefill. Its stride-aligned source assignment is engineering-friendly and naturally compatible with PP/VPP schedules, making the design suitable for large-scale distributed training. 4). Consistent empirical gains. We validate DepthGraft on both dense and MoE models, covering model scales from 0.5B to 16B total parameters. Across scales and attention variants, DepthGraft consistently improves downstream performance while preserving inference efficiency. 2. Related Work Cross-layer connectivity. broad line of work enriches depth-wise information flow by giving each layer direct access to earlier representations [15, 17, 18]. DenseNet [15] concatenates all preceding feature maps, establishing canonical dense cross-layer design. In Transformers, DenseFormer [23] and ANCRe [45] introduce learned layer-wise connection weights, while Value Residual Learning [47] adds targeted residual access to earlier value states. Attention Residuals [33] replaces fixed residual accumulation with learned reweighting over preceding hidden states, and MoDA [48] augments sequence attention with keyvalue memories from previous layers. Together, these works show that cross-layer connectivity is an effective mechanism for improving deep Transformer architectures [25, 44]. KV sharing for efficient inference. KV cache is major memory bottleneck during autoregressive inference, motivating many methods that reduce cache storage through KV sharing [37, 38, 43]. Cross-layer KV sharing is an important direction in this line. CLA [4] and MLKV [49] reuse KV within adjacent layer groups, reducing cache but often incurring performance degradation when the reuse constraint becomes too strong. YOCO [31] shares global KV memory for all deeper layers, enabling prefill early completion and strong cache reduction. FusedKV [20] further reconstructs deep-layer KV from two global anchors, providing more flexibility than direct global reuse. Cross-layer KV sharing is becoming an increasingly important architectural choice for large-scale LLM pretraining, as illustrated by its adoption in DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash [41] and HySparse2 [35]. Positioning. DepthGraft systematically analyzes how cross-layer KV sharing alters training dynamics, showing that the induced cross-layer gradients can regularize KV representation geometry. Guided by this analysis, DepthGraft uses stride-aligned hierarchical reconstruction to improve KV representations and model quality while preserving the KV-cache savings of sharing-based inference. 3. DepthGraft: Hierarchical Cross-Layer KV Reconstruction By viewing KV-sharing designs through the lens of cross-layer gradients as structural regularization, the analysis above motivates the following design principles: 1. Sufficient cross-layer distance. Source and reuse layers must be separated by enough depth that their query spaces meaningfully diverge, enabling the gradient interference that drives K/V specialization. Adjacent-layer sharing fails this condition. 2. Distributed gradient flow with full-layer participation. Each source layer should receive gradients from only small number of reuse layers to avoid gradient congestion, and most layers should participate in the cross-layer connectivity graph so that the regularization benefit is not confined to few anchors. We instantiate these requirements under an efficiency constraint: all source KV tensors should be produced before the reconstructed layers, preserving prefill early completion. Based on this, we propose DepthGraft, which introduces hierarchical stage layout that partitions the 𝐿-layer Transformer into shallow, middle, and deep stages, each containing roughly 𝐿/3 layers. The shallow and middle stages compute KV normally, while the deep stage reconstructs its KV from earlier stages. Rather than using global anchors, DepthGraft adopts stride-aligned source assignment, treating deep-layer memory as locally reconstructed trajectory over depth. Because the deep stage does not materialize independent KV, DepthGraft reduces the KV cache and prefill cost by approximately 1/3. The stride-aligned source mapping is simple to implement and naturally compatible with pipeline parallelism (PP) and virtual pipeline parallelism (VPP), avoiding additional cross-stage KV communication under an appropriate placement. Appendix F.3 provides the corresponding PP/VPP details. (3) Regularized KV geometry. The design satisfies the two principles above: non-local sourcetarget pairs provide query-space separation, and stride alignment distributes cross-layer gradients across source layers. As shown in Fig. 2 and Fig. 3(b), DepthGraft improves the geometry of KV representations while maintaining healthy distributed gradient flow. Experiments We evaluate DepthGraft on both dense and sparse MoE Transformers, covering multiple model scales and attention variants. Our experiments are organized around three questions: (1) whether the empirical results support the analysis in Sec. 3.2, i.e., whether DepthGraft can use cross-layer gradients as structural regularizer to improve downstream performance while preserving the KV-cache and prefill-efficiency benefits of KV sharing; (2) whether this effect scales to larger models and remains effective across different attention variants; and (3) whether the cross-layer connectivity and stage-layout choices in Sec. 3.4 are necessary, and how alternative sharing variants behave under the same training and evaluation protocol. 4.1. DepthGraft improves the average score at all three scales, by +0.75, +0.85, and +2.42 points, respectively. The gains are not confined to single benchmark family. At 1.5B, for example, DepthGraft improves knowledge understanding (MMLU +3.33, MMLU-Pro +1.43), reasoning and mathematics (SIQA +2.86, GSM8K +0.91), code generation (MBPP +5.20), and Chinese comprehension (C3 +9.46). This consistent improvement on dense models indicates that constraining only the KV memory pathway does not reduce model capacity; instead, it provides useful inductive bias for deep-layer memory representations. MoE models. We next scale DepthGraft to MoE architectures from 3B to 16B total parameters  (Table 2)  . Across GQA-based MoE models, DepthGraft consistently outperforms the corresponding baseline, improving the average score by +1.05, +2.29, and +3.61 points at 3B, 9B, and 16B, respectively. The 16B model shows especially strong gains, including MMLU-Pro (+7.00), CMMLU (+6.61), C3 (+6.41), and GSM8K (+5.84). Furthermore, the consistent gains on both 9B GQA (+2.29 Avg.) and 9B MLA (+3.68 Avg.) further show that DepthGraft is not tied to particular attention implementation. Taken together, the main results support the mechanism developed in Sec. 3.2: cross-layer KV reconstruction improves performance not merely by saving cache, but by reshaping the geometry of KV representations through direct cross-layer gradient regularization. The fact that the gains appear across dense models, sparse MoE models, different attention variants, and wide range of scales suggests that the effect is stable architectural bias rather than scalespecific artifact. During training, we also observe that the cross-layer gradient regularization introduced by DepthGraft can weaken attention-sink behavior, further supporting the view that DepthGraft improves the organization of the memory pathway. Conclusion and Future Work We presented DepthGraft, hierarchical cross-layer KV reconstruction method that turns KV sharing from cache-saving mechanism into regularized memory pathway. Our analysis shows that KV reuse creates direct cross-layer gradient paths that reshape KV representation geometry, and that the effectiveness of this regularization depends on the topology of the sharing graph. Motivated by this view, DepthGraft reconstructs deep-layer KV from stride-aligned shallowmiddle source pairs, preserving the efficiency benefits of KV sharing while distributing non-local gradient flow across source layers. Experiments on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B show consistent downstream gains, substantial reductions in KV cache and prefill cost, and negligible overhead during decoding. Future work can develop more rigorous theoretical understanding of how cross-layer KV sharing improves representation geometry, explore more effective sharing topologies, and further scale this direction to larger pretraining regimes.

The shallow and middle stages compute and cache KV normally, while deep-stage KV is reconstructed from stride-aligned shallowmiddle source pairs. The deep stage therefore does not materialize independent KV cache, while gradients from deep-layer attention flow back to the source KV projections through the reconstruction paths. RoPE-pair tying for coefficients. Rotary position embeddings apply block-diagonal rotation to each two-dimensional channel pair of the query and key vectors. For the NeoX-style layout used in our implementation, dimensions 𝑗 and 𝑗 + 𝑑/2 form one RoPE pair. If channel-wise coefficient assigns different values to the two dimensions in the same pair, then applying RoPE before and after reconstruction would no longer be equivalent. Attention Sink Analysis common pathology in deep Transformers is the attention sink phenomenon, where disproportionate amount of attention mass is assigned to the first token regardless of its semantic relevance [39]. In our setting, this behavior provides an additional diagnostic of key geometry: if layer develops extreme key directions, the softmax distribution can become dominated by small number of sink positions. DepthGraft mitigates this tendency through cross-layer gradient regularization. Each shallow or middle source serves its own attention layer while also being reused by stride-aligned deep layer, so its KV projections receive optimization signals from multiple query spaces. This structure can regularize the source key geometry and make it less likely for layer to develop sink-prone key directions that dominate the softmax. This is consistent with the analysis in Sec. 3.2, where useful cross-layer KV sharing makes keys form more compact retrieval geometry. We verify this empirically by tracking the average attention score assigned to the first token throughout training. Figure 6 reports this metric for both 9B GQA and 9B MLA models. In both cases, DepthGraft consistently lowers first-token attention concentration relative to the baseline, indicating reduced attention-sink behavior. E.3. The shallow and middle stages materialize KV normally, while the deep stage reconstructs its KV from stride-aligned shallowmiddle sources. Therefore, no independent KV cache needs to be stored for the deep stage. For an 𝐿-layer model with identical KV dimensionality across layers, the baseline stores KV for all 𝐿 layers, whereas DepthGraft stores KV only for roughly 2𝐿/3 source layers: KVCache𝐷𝑒𝑝𝑡ℎ𝐺𝑟𝑎 𝑓 𝑡 KVCachebaseline 2𝐿/3 𝐿 = 2 3 . (33) This gives an approximately one-third reduction in KV-cache memory during inference. The same structure also enables prefill early completion. In standard autoregressive inference, the prefill phase processes the full prompt through all layers to produce the KV cache and the hidden state needed to generate the first response token. In DepthGraft, the purpose of prefill with respect to KV construction is completed once the shallow and middle stages have processed the full prompt, because all KV tensors needed by future decoding steps have already been materialized. The deep stage does not need to process the entire prompt to create additional KV cache. Instead, after the shallow and middle KV caches are available, we only forward the final prompt token through the deep stage, using the stored shallowmiddle KV caches to compute attention and produce the first response token. Thus, the prefill saving comes from avoiding full-sequence computation in the deep stage, while retaining the necessary computation for the last prompt token that initializes decoding. As context length and model size increase, the full-prompt prefill computation becomes increasingly dominant, and the cost of forwarding only the final token through the deep stage becomes smaller fraction of total prefill cost. This explains the trend in Table 3: the measured TTFT reduction grows at longer context lengths and approaches the theoretical one-third saving. 26 F.2. Parallel Training Compatibility Pipeline parallelism (PP) is essential for training large Transformers whose parameters and activations cannot fit on single device. PP partitions the model along depth and assigns different layer blocks to different physical pipeline ranks. Virtual pipeline parallelism (VPP) further splits each physical stage into smaller virtual chunks, typically at layer granularity, and interleaves their execution to reduce pipeline bubbles and improve hardware utilization. For cross-layer KV sharing, the main systems concern is whether reuse layer needs to fetch source KV tensors from different PP rank; such accesses would introduce additional cross-stage communication and complicate activation lifetime management. DepthGraft is designed to avoid this issue. Because each deep layer reuses stride-aligned shallowmiddle source pair, the source and reuse layers can be co-located on the same physical PP rank under an appropriate VPP partition. Table 12 gives balanced example for 36-layer model with PP size 4. Using zero-based layer indices, the network is divided into three 12-layer stages: layers 011, 1223, and 2435. Each deep layer 𝑖 + 24 reconstructs KV from the stridealigned pair (𝑖, 𝑖 + 12), and each triple (𝑖, 𝑖 + 12, 𝑖 + 24) is placed on the same physical PP rank. Thus, cross-layer KV production and consumption remain local to one device. This layout preserves the natural forward order as three repeated PP passes over shallow, middle, and deep depth bands, while keeping the non-local KV dependency local within each physical rank.
